title: Joshua 10:16–27
context: The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua has it sealed while the army pursues the fleeing troops, then brings the kings out. His captains put their feet on the kings’ necks as Joshua repeats the charge to be strong and courageous. The kings are executed, hung on trees until evening in line with Deuteronomy 21:22–23, and buried in the cave, which is sealed with great stones.

verses.text: These five kings fled, and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah.
verses.arminianNotes: The five kings flee and hide in the cave at Makkedah. Arminian readers note the reversal: kings who gathered to destroy Gibeon now hide in fear, as the coalition collapses under the LORD’s hand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as the humbling of proud rulers, a pattern found throughout Scripture. Both traditions note that Makkedah, where the cave lies, is a site whose exact location is still uncertain.

verses.text: Joshua was told, saying, “The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua receives the report that the kings have been found. Arminian readers note the steady flow of information in the account and the way the leaders’ hiding place is quickly discovered by Israel’s men.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the discovery God’s providence leaving the enemy no refuge. Shared ground: the verse moves the story from the battle to the fate of the kings, setting up Joshua’s next instructions.

verses.text: Joshua said, “Roll large stones to cover the cave’s entrance, and set men by it to guard them;
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua orders large stones rolled over the cave entrance with guards set. Arminian readers see practical leadership, securing the kings so that the army can continue pursuing the fleeing troops.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the sealed cave keeps the kings captive until the right time for judgment. Both traditions agree that Joshua’s command shows discipline: he puts the main task of pursuit ahead of dealing with the captured leaders.

verses.text: but don’t stay there. Pursue your enemies, and attack them from the rear. Don’t allow them to enter into their cities; for the LORD your God has delivered them into your hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua tells the troops to pursue and keep the enemy from reaching their cities, for the LORD has given them over. Arminian readers note the combination of urgency and confidence in his orders to the army.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Joshua’s assurance rooted in God’s promise in 10:8. Shared ground: the command to keep going rests on the conviction that the LORD has already delivered the enemy, so Israel must act on that promise without delay.

verses.text: When Joshua and the children of Israel had finished killing them with a very great slaughter until they were consumed, and the remnant which remained of them had entered into the fortified cities,
verses.arminianNotes: Israel defeats the enemy with great slaughter, though a remnant reaches fortified cities. Arminian readers note the honesty of the account, which admits that some survivors escaped despite the scale of the victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the survivors in fortified cities as setting up the campaign that follows in 10:28–39. Both traditions observe that the text’s own detail of a remnant shows that the language of total victory is not meant to cover every individual.

verses.text: all the people returned to the camp to Joshua at Makkedah in peace. None moved his tongue against any of the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The army returns to Joshua at Makkedah in peace, and no one dares to speak against Israel. Arminian readers note that the phrase about moving the tongue points to the fear now gripping the surrounding peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the silence of the nations as fruit of the LORD’s victory, recalling Exodus 11:7. Shared ground: the verse marks a moment of calm and security after battle, granted to Israel by the LORD.

verses.text: Then Joshua said, “Open the cave entrance, and bring those five kings out of the cave to me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua orders the cave opened and the five kings brought out. Arminian readers note the public nature of what follows, as Israel’s leader brings captured rulers before the people rather than dealing with them in secret.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the kings brought into the light for judgment that the community will witness. Both traditions agree that the scene is staged as a public lesson about the LORD’s victory and Israel’s calling.

verses.text: They did so, and brought those five kings out of the cave to him: the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.
verses.arminianNotes: The kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon are brought out. Arminian readers note that the narrator repeats the list from 10:3 and 10:5, closing the circle on the coalition that attacked Gibeon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as emphasizing that every king who rose against God’s people now stands defeated. Shared ground: the list ties the end of the story back to its beginning, so readers see the whole alliance brought low.

verses.text: When they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua called for all the men of Israel, and said to the chiefs of the men of war who went with him, “Come near. Put your feet on the necks of these kings.” They came near, and put their feet on their necks.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua’s chiefs put their feet on the kings’ necks. Arminian readers recognize an ancient gesture of conquest, used to encourage soldiers who would face these kings’ cities and peoples in the days ahead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the gesture as a sign of total subjection, an image that later appears in passages such as Psalm 110:1, where enemies become a footstool. Both traditions read the act as symbolic and aimed at building Israel’s courage.

verses.text: Joshua said to them, “Don’t be afraid, nor be dismayed. Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all your enemies against whom you fight.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua tells them not to fear but to be strong and courageous. Arminian readers note that he passes on to his officers the charge God gave him in 1:6–9, so the leader’s encouragement becomes the army’s own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise that the LORD will do this to all their enemies as grounding courage in God’s action. Shared ground: the charge looks ahead to the rest of the conquest, with confidence resting on the LORD rather than on Israel’s strength.

verses.text: Afterward Joshua struck them, put them to death, and hanged them on five trees. They were hanging on the trees until the evening.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua puts the kings to death and hangs their bodies on five trees until evening. Arminian readers state the act plainly, noting that the text presents it as judgment on rulers who led the war against Gibeon and Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same practice with the king of Ai (8:29), and see Joshua following the law’s limits on public display. Both traditions read the execution within the conquest’s unique setting rather than as a pattern for today.

verses.text: At the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down off the trees, and threw them into the cave in which they had hidden themselves, and laid great stones on the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.
verses.arminianNotes: At sunset the bodies are taken down and placed in the cave, which is sealed with great stones that remain to this very day. Arminian readers see Joshua obeying Deuteronomy 21:22–23 by not leaving bodies hanging overnight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the stone heap serves as a memorial of the LORD’s victory, like other markers in Joshua. Shared ground: the narrator’s phrase “to this very day” points to a landmark known to later readers of the account.
